summary: Looks at the shortcomings of existing localized mobility solutions, which all involve the host, and makes the case for network-based localized mobility management. This memo is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When a device moves between wireless access points, something has to keep the connection alive. The older methods all need software changes inside the device. This memo argues for moving that work into the network instead, so that any device can roam inside one access network.

questions: what is the difference between local and global mobility
why is network-based mobility management useful
subtitle: Why a moving device should not need mobility software to move between access points in one access network.

tldr.problem: Every localized mobility protocol the IETF had produced needed the device to run extra IP software, and the devices of the future may not be running Mobile IPv6 at all.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets out the local mobility problem, the three known costs of handling a small move with a global mobility protocol, and the scenarios where localized management is wanted. It then compares the two existing classes of solution with a network-based approach that keeps the work in the access network.
tldr.outcome: The document is a problem statement, not a specification. It points at RFC 4831 for the goals of a network-based protocol and RFC 4832 for the threats to the same architecture.

facts.label: Problems listed for the IP-level class

today: RFC 4830 is an Informational document published in April 2007, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a problem statement rather than a specification: the goals for a network-based protocol are in RFC 4831, and the threats to the same architecture are covered in RFC 4832.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
Localized mobility management has had a lot of work at the IETF. The experimental protocols that came out of it, Fast Handovers for Mobile IPv6 (RFC 4068) and Hierarchical Mobile IPv6 (RFC 4140), all involve the host and need host involvement at the IP layer, like Mobile IPv6 (RFC 3775) or in addition to it. The RFC argues that it is time to look at the problem again.

Two things have changed. New global mobility work at the IETF, such as the Host Identity Protocol (RFC 4423) and MOBIKE (RFC 4555), suggests that future wireless nodes may support a more diverse set of global mobility protocols, and the existing localized protocols would need extra work to implement, deploy or even specify outside a Mobile IPv6 environment. Second, WLAN switches, which do localized management with no host stack involvement at all, have succeeded in the market, which points at a paradigm that could accommodate other global mobility options while reducing host stack software complexity and widening the range of nodes that could be served.

The document describes the local mobility problem and the scenarios where localized management would be wanted, lists the problems with existing or proposed IETF protocols, and presents the network-based mobility management architecture and a short description of how it solves them. RFC 4831 (RFC 4831) holds the goals for such a protocol and the gap analysis for existing protocols. IPv6 and wireless links are the initial scope, so the language of the document reflects that, but the conclusions apply equally to IPv4 and to wired links, where nodes disconnect and reconnect.
sections.plainLanguage: When a device moves between wireless access points, somebody has to keep the connection alive. The older methods all need software changes in the device. This memo argues for moving that work into the network instead.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
The memo follows the mobility vocabulary of RFC 3753 and adds terms of its own. A WLAN switch is a multiport Ethernet switch that connects network segments and runs a protocol to control a collection of 802.11 access points, which lets it perform radio resource management functions such as power control and terminal load balancing between those access points. Most WLAN switches also support a proprietary protocol for inter-subnet IP mobility, usually involving some kind of inter-switch IP tunnel, which provides session continuity when a terminal moves between subnets.

An access network is a collection of fixed and mobile network components allowing access to the Internet, all belonging to a single operational domain. It may mix several air interface technologies, such as 802.16e or UMTS, with several kinds of backhaul interconnection, such as SONET or metro Ethernet.

Local mobility is mobility over an access network. The area of network topology the node moves over may be restricted, but the actual geographic area could still be large, depending on how network topology maps onto wireless coverage. Localized mobility management is any protocol that maintains the IP connectivity and reachability of a mobile node, for the sake of session continuity when the node moves, and whose signaling is confined to an access network. A global mobility management protocol is a protocol the mobile node uses to change the global, end-to-end routing of packets when movement invalidates its global unicast address; it could be Mobile IP, HIP or MOBIKE. The global mobility anchor point is the node where the mobile node keeps a permanent address and the mapping to the temporary address where it currently is. Intra-link mobility is movement between access points within one link, usually handled by layer 2 mechanisms, so no IP subnet configuration is needed on movement; if a link is served by a single access point and router, that kind of mobility is typically absent.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo borrows the standard mobility words and adds a few of its own. The key distinction is between moving inside one link, moving inside one access network, and moving between access networks, which is the only case that needs a heavyweight protocol.

sections.title: The Local Mobility Problem
sections.content:
The local mobility problem is restricted to providing IP mobility management for mobile nodes within an access network. The access network gateways function as aggregation routers. There is no specialized routing protocol such as GTP, Cellular IP or Hawaii; the routers form a standard IP routed network running OSPF, IS-IS or RIP. Transitions between service providers in separate autonomous systems, or across broader topological boundaries within one provider, are excluded.

The RFC's figure splits movement into three kinds. Moving between two access points under the same access router is intra-link, or layer 2, mobility, usually handled by layer 2 mobility protocols. Moving between two access points connected to two different access routers is local mobility. Moving between two access networks needs a global mobility protocol, which works by updating the mapping between the permanent address and the temporary local address at the global mobility anchor point, or even end to end by changing the temporary local address directly at the correspondent node.

A global mobility protocol can therefore be used between access routers to handle local mobility, but the RFC names three problems with doing that for every move. First, update latency: if the anchor point or the correspondent node for route-optimized traffic is at a distance from the mobile node's access network, the update can take a considerable amount of time, and during that time packets continue to be routed to the old temporary local address and are essentially dropped. Second, signaling overhead: moving from one last-hop link to another needs signaling to configure an IP address on the new link and global mobility protocol signaling back into the network to change the mapping, and that volume may hurt wireless bandwidth usage and real-time service performance. Third, location privacy: the change of temporary local address exposes the mobile node's topological location to correspondents and potentially to eavesdroppers, and an attacker able to assemble a mapping between subnet prefixes and geographical locations can determine exactly where the node is.
sections.plainLanguage: These problems are why the memo wants small moves handled locally. Doing every move the heavyweight way means waiting for a distant server before traffic flows again, a lot of signalling on the radio link, and telling everybody roughly where the device is.

sections.title: Scenarios for Localized Mobility Management
sections.content:
A large campus is one case where localized mobility management would be attractive. When the geographical span of the campus, the distribution of buildings and the availability of wiring rule out deploying all WLAN access points as part of the same IP subnet, WLAN layer 2 mobility cannot be used across the entire campus. The campus is then divided into separate last-hop links, each served by one or more access routers. This is served today by WLAN switches that coordinate IP mobility between them, effectively providing localized mobility management at the link layer. Because the protocols are proprietary and do not interoperate, any deployment that requires IP mobility has to use switches from the same vendor.

An advanced cellular network is the second scenario. Next-generation cellular protocols such as 802.16e and Super 3G could run IP deeper into the access network than current 3G protocols do, in the way today's WLAN networks already do, so the access network becomes a routed IP network. An interoperable localized mobility management protocol could unify local mobility across advanced cellular, WLAN and personal area wireless technologies such as UWB and Bluetooth, all served by IP. Localized mobility management at the IP layer does not replace layer 2 mobility where it exists, it complements it. A standardized, interoperable protocol removes the dependence on IP-layer protocols that are specialized to specific link technologies or proprietary, which is the situation with today's 3G protocols, and the expected benefit is a reduction in maintenance cost and deployment complexity.

The third scenario is a picocellular network with small but node-dense last-hop links. Future radio link protocols at very high frequencies may be constrained to very short, line-of-sight operation, and some existing protocols such as UWB and Bluetooth are designed for low transmit power and short-range operation, which makes extremely small picocells more practical. Although picocells do not necessarily mean small subnets, wireless sensors and other advanced applications may end up making such networks node-dense, with subnets covering small geographical areas such as a single room. Being able to aggregate many subnets under a localized mobility management scheme helps reduce the amount of IP signaling required on link movement.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo gives three situations where this matters: a campus too big for one subnet, cellular networks that start carrying IP the way Wi-Fi already does, and tiny short-range cells packed with sensors where each move would otherwise cost a lot of signalling.

sections.title: Existing Solutions and the Network-Based Alternative
sections.content:
Existing solutions fall into two classes. The first is interoperable IP-level protocols that require changes to the mobile node's IP stack and handle localized mobility management as a service the access network provides to the node. The second is link-specific or proprietary protocols that handle localized mobility for any mobile node but only for one type of link layer, for example 802.11.

The dedicated IETF protocols in the first class are not yet widely deployed, although standardization work continues, and some Mobile IPv4 deployments use localized mobility management. They have four specific problems. The host stack software requirement limits broad usage even when the modifications are small, because operators and users clearly prefer no host stack changes, as the success of WLAN switches indicates. Every existing localized solution depends on Mobile IP or a derivative, so a node that picks another global mobility management protocol, such as HIP or MOBIKE, is left out. None of them supports both IPv4 and IPv6. And host-based solutions require setting up additional security associations with network elements in the access domain.

The proprietary class has been widely accepted and is still growing, but it has three problems. Those solutions only support WLAN networks with Ethernet backhaul, so they are not available for advanced cellular networks, picocellular protocols or other types of wired backhaul. Each WLAN switch vendor has its own proprietary protocol that does not interoperate with other vendors' equipment. And because the solutions are based on layer 2 routing, they may not scale up to a metropolitan area or a local province, particularly when multiple kinds of link technologies are used in the backbone.

The memo's answer is an interoperable, standardized localized mobility management protocol that is scalable to topologically large networks but requires no host stack involvement. Compared with the first class it needs no localized mobility management support on the node and is independent of the global mobility management protocol, so it can be used with any of them or with none, which gives a more modular architecture that better accommodates changing technology and market requirements. Compared with the second class, an IP-level network-based solution works for link protocols other than Ethernet and for wide area networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Today's fixes come in two flavours: standard IP protocols that need changes in the device, and vendor-specific tricks that work only for Wi-Fi. The memo backs a standard IP protocol that the device knows nothing about, so it works over any kind of link and alongside any global mobility scheme.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Localized mobility management has certain security considerations, one of which, the need for security from the access network to the mobile node, was discussed in the document. Host-based localized mobility management protocols carry all the security problems involved with providing a service to a host. Network-based localized mobility management instead requires security among network elements that is equivalent to what is needed for routing information security, and security between the host and the network that is equivalent to what is needed for network access, but no more. The RFC points to RFC 4831 for a more complete discussion of the security goals for network-based localized mobility management.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the network does the work, the security burden moves with it: the network elements have to trust each other, and the device has to be authenticated to the network as usual. Nothing extra is demanded of the device.

items.text: Between access networks; needs a protocol that changes the end-to-end routing.
